course.title: Phishing Investigation
course.description: A practical intermediate course for investigating suspected phishing from user report through evidence preservation, standards-based email analysis, authentication review, URL and attachment triage, identity and mailbox correlation, campaign scoping, containment validation, detection improvement, and defensible reporting. Students use controlled artifacts and synthetic telemetry rather than real credentials or live attacker infrastructure.
prerequisites: Basic TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, and SMTP knowledge
Basic Windows or Linux command-line skills
A safe lab environment for controlled phishing artifacts
learningOutcomes: triage phishing reports and preserve original evidence
analyze email structure, routing, identity, and authentication fields
parse and normalize suspicious URLs safely
preserve and hash attachment artifacts with provenance
correlate phishing evidence with identity and mailbox telemetry
map observed delivery methods to MITRE ATT&CK
design proportionate containment and validation procedures
produce structured phishing indicators and handling metadata
write technical and executive phishing investigation reports with confidence and limitations

modules.title: Investigation Foundations
modules.description: Build the investigation mindset: scope the event, preserve evidence, classify phishing, and triage risk before technical deep-dives.

lessons.title: Case Questions and Evidence Logic
lessons.description: Turn a phishing report into explicit hypotheses and evidence questions.
learningObjectives: identify minimum evidence needed to support a phishing assessment

notes.text: Observation vs conclusion

An investigation should distinguish what was directly observed from what the analyst concludes. A user saying “I clicked it” is an important lead; a browser or secure-link event can corroborate it. A suspicious display name is an observation; “the sender is malicious” is a conclusion that needs more evidence.

items: Ask whether the message was delivered, interacted with, and followed by security-relevant events.
Record which evidence would increase or decrease confidence.
Treat case scope as changeable as new evidence arrives.

practicals.title: Build a Phishing Case Intake Record
practicals.description: Create a structured intake record that preserves the submitted artifact identity while separating initial suspicion from established facts.
steps: Record the original artifact filename and acquisition context.
Record investigator action time separately from any message timestamp.
Calculate a SHA-256 digest of the original artifact without editing it.
Write a scope statement that distinguishes confirmed facts from hypotheses.
practicals.solution:
from pathlib import Path
import hashlib

path = Path("reported-message.eml")
data = path.read_bytes()
record = {
    "artifact": path.name,
    "sha256": hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest(),
    "scope": "Assess whether the submitted message is phishing and determine affected scope.",
    "status": "intake-complete"
}
print(record)
practicals.output: A reproducible intake record containing the artifact name, SHA-256 digest, investigation scope, and case state.

quiz.question: Which statement is an evidence-based finding?
options: The sender is definitely a criminal.
Multiple independent observations support a high-confidence phishing assessment.
The domain is unfamiliar, so it is malicious.
quiz.answer: Multiple independent observations support a high-confidence phishing assessment.
quiz.explanation: A finding should connect an assessment to evidence and confidence.

summary: Phishing investigation is structured hypothesis testing.
Evidence traceability is more important than dramatic wording.

lessons.title: Phishing Taxonomy and ATT&CK
lessons.description: Classify attachment, link, service, and voice phishing and distinguish delivery from later behaviors.
learningObjectives: identify T1566 and its current sub-techniques
classify a message by observed delivery mechanism

notes.text: MITRE ATT&CK models Phishing as T1566 with sub-techniques for spearphishing attachment, link, service, and voice. The delivery classification should not be confused with later behaviors such as credential access, execution, or persistence.

items: Use T1566.002 when the investigated delivery mechanism is a spearphishing link.
Use T1566.001 when the delivery mechanism is a spearphishing attachment.
Map later actions only when evidence supports them.

quiz.question: A suspicious email primarily delivers a credential-harvesting URL. Which ATT&CK sub-technique best describes the delivery?
quiz.explanation: T1566.002 is Spearphishing Link.

summary: ATT&CK is a behavioral classification framework, not an attribution engine.
The observed delivery method determines the phishing sub-technique.

lessons.title: Triage, Priority, and Preservation
lessons.description: Decide what to protect and collect first based on potential impact and evidence volatility.
learningObjectives: identify evidence likely to disappear or change

notes.text: Early triage can consider privileged accounts, possible credential exposure, campaign breadth, and the availability window of mail and identity telemetry. NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 places incident response within broader cybersecurity risk management and emphasizes efficient detection, response, and recovery.

items: Preserve the original message/export before editing it.
Record message identifiers and timestamps early.
Do not turn an unverified user recollection into a factual conclusion.

quiz.question: What most directly protects the evidentiary source during initial triage?
options: Preserving the original export and identifiers
quiz.answer: Preserving the original export and identifiers
quiz.explanation: Preserving source data before manipulation reduces the risk of losing or altering evidence.

summary: Preservation and prioritization happen before deep interpretation.
Escalation should be explainable from recorded risk.

tasks.title: Create a Phishing Case Intake Record
tasks.description: Build a structured case record from a minimal user report.
tasks.problemStatement: Capture source, scope, message identifiers, priority, hypotheses, and preservation needs for one controlled case.
tasks.hint: Start with evidence identifiers and keep derived assessments separate.
tasks.solutionCode:
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
import hashlib, json

@dataclass
class Case:
    case_id: str
    source: str
    priority: str
    message_id: str
    sha256: str
    hypotheses: list

raw = b"controlled-phishing-artifact"
case = Case("PHISH-001", "user-submitted", "High", "<controlled@example.invalid>", hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest(), ["benign", "impersonation", "credential theft"])
print(json.dumps(asdict(case), indent=2))
tasks.solutionExplanation: The structure preserves source identity and makes the hypotheses explicit instead of hiding them in a free-form verdict.

modules.title: Email Anatomy and Header Analysis
modules.description: Read standards-based message structure and analyze routing, identity, and authentication headers without overclaiming.

lessons.title: RFC 5322 Message Structure
lessons.description: Understand the message header/body model and the difference between content syntax and transport behavior.
learningObjectives: explain header fields and message body
distinguish RFC 5322 from SMTP transport details

notes.text: RFC 5322 specifies Internet message format: header fields followed by an optional body. Transport-envelope behavior is addressed by other mail protocols, so an analyst must not infer every transport fact from message content alone.

From: Finance Support <support@example.invalid>
To: analyst@example.invalid
Message-ID: <abc123@example.invalid>
Subject: Review required

items: Message-ID supports correlation but is not sender authentication.
Date describes origination context, not necessarily delivery time.
Received fields provide trace information that should be interpreted within a trust model.

quiz.question: What does RFC 5322 primarily specify?
quiz.answer: Internet message format
quiz.explanation: RFC 5322 specifies Internet message format, including headers and body syntax.

summary: Preserve the complete source message.
Message content syntax is not the entire mail-delivery history.

lessons.title: Received Header Reasoning
lessons.description: Use Received fields to construct a cautious delivery timeline.

notes.text: Received fields can support path reconstruction, but each entry reflects a processing point and its trust context. A gateway or provider log can corroborate routing observations when exact provenance matters.

items: Preserve header order and raw text.
Do not label the first visible address as “the attacker IP” without corroboration.
Compare timestamps and infrastructure ownership with trusted logs.

notes.text: Routing fields can originate outside your administrative trust boundary. They are useful evidence, not self-authenticating proof.

practicals.title: Extract Routing Headers from EML
practicals.description: Parse a controlled EML file and inspect routing and identity headers without executing links or attachments.
steps: Place a controlled EML file in the lab directory.
Parse it using Python's email package with policy.default.
Print selected identity fields and every Received header.
Record observations without treating a single header as proof of maliciousness.
practicals.solution:
from email import policy
from email.parser import BytesParser

with open("lab.eml", "rb") as fh:
    message = BytesParser(policy=policy.default).parse(fh)

for field in ("From", "To", "Reply-To", "Return-Path", "Message-ID"):
    print(f"{field}: {message.get(field)}")

for index, received in enumerate(message.get_all("Received", []), 1):
    print(f"Received[{index}]: {received}")
practicals.output: The console displays the selected identity fields and the Received chain for manual routing analysis.

quiz.question: Why corroborate a suspicious Received header with gateway logs?
options: Some routing information can originate outside the organization’s trust boundary
quiz.answer: Some routing information can originate outside the organization’s trust boundary
quiz.explanation: Corroboration reduces the chance of treating an untrusted or incomplete trace as definitive.

summary: Routing analysis works best as a chain of corroborated observations.
Trust-boundary reasoning is essential.

lessons.title: Authentication-Results and Domain Authentication
lessons.description: Interpret SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Authentication-Results in context.
learningObjectives: state what authentication results do not prove

notes.text: RFC 8601 defines Authentication-Results as a message header that records authentication evaluation results. SPF evaluates authorized sending hosts for a domain; DKIM verifies a cryptographic signature; DMARC evaluates alignment between authenticated domains and the visible From domain. A passing result is useful evidence, but it does not guarantee benign intent.
Authentication-Results: mx.example.invalid; spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=example.invalid; dkim=fail header.d=example.invalid; dmarc=fail header.from=example.invalid

items: Record the exact result and domain.
Explain alignment separately from basic pass/fail values.
Consider compromised legitimate accounts and trusted services as possible phishing sources.

quiz.question: What is Authentication-Results?
options: A receiver-side header recording authentication evaluation results
quiz.answer: A receiver-side header recording authentication evaluation results
quiz.explanation: RFC 8601 defines this message header for conveying authentication results.

summary: Authentication results are analytical inputs, not a universal safety label.
Domain identity must be interpreted alongside content and infrastructure evidence.

lessons.title: Identity Fields and Impersonation
lessons.description: Compare From, Reply-To, Return-Path, display identity, and Message-ID.

notes.text: Phishing messages can use deceptive display names, lookalike domains, Reply-To changes, and familiar branding. Investigators should compare identity fields against authentication results and provider telemetry rather than declaring spoofing from one mismatch.

From: Finance Team <finance@trusted.invalid>
Reply-To: finance-help@untrusted.invalid
Return-Path: bounce@mailer.untrusted.invalid
Message-ID: <7f2a@example.invalid>

quiz.question: Which field directly identifies the suggested reply destination?
quiz.answer: Reply-To
quiz.explanation: RFC 5322 defines Reply-To as the address(es) to which replies are suggested to be sent.

summary: Visible identity, reply identity, and envelope identity can differ legitimately or maliciously.
Mismatches are leads that require context.

tasks.title: Parse and Normalize an EML Artifact
tasks.description: Parse a preserved EML file and output investigation-relevant fields.
tasks.problemStatement: Extract key identity/authentication headers, preserve every Received field, and hash the source bytes.
objectives: parse the EML with Python’s email package
tasks.hint: Use BytesParser with a standard policy and get_all() for repeated headers.
tasks.solutionCode:
from email import policy
from email.parser import BytesParser

with open("evidence.eml", "rb") as fh:
    message = BytesParser(policy=policy.default).parse(fh)

for field in ("From", "To", "Reply-To", "Return-Path", "Subject", "Date", "Message-ID", "Authentication-Results"):
    print(f"{field}: {message.get(field)}")

for index, received in enumerate(message.get_all("Received", []), 1):
    print(f"Received[{index}]: {received}")
tasks.solutionExplanation: The parser creates a reproducible evidence view without altering the original source file.

modules.title: URL and Web Infrastructure Analysis
modules.description: Investigate links and domains safely, separating exact source URLs from normalized analytical views.

lessons.title: URL Structure and Canonicalization
lessons.description: Break suspicious URLs into components and retain the exact original string.
learningObjectives: parse scheme, host, port, path, query

notes.text: URL investigation benefits from two views: the untouched source string and a normalized representation used for comparison. Analysts should watch for userinfo, misleading subdomains, encoding, and unnecessary redirect layers.
https://login.example.invalid@untrusted.invalid/session?next=%2Fhome

items: The hostname in the controlled example is untrusted.invalid.
Canonicalization should be stored as a derived value.
Never replace the original evidence with a normalized version.

practicals.title: Normalize a Suspicious URL Offline
practicals.description: Decompose a controlled URL locally so the analyst can identify the effective hostname and other components without contacting the site.
steps: Define a controlled URL string.
Parse it with urllib.parse.urlsplit.
Record hostname, username presence, port, path, and query.
Do not fetch the URL or submit credentials.
practicals.solution:
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

raw_url = "https://login.example.invalid@untrusted.invalid:8443/session?next=%2Fhome"
parts = urlsplit(raw_url)
record = {
    "hostname": parts.hostname,
    "username_present": bool(parts.username),
    "port": parts.port,
    "path": parts.path,
    "query": parts.query,
}
print(record)
practicals.output: A local parse showing the effective hostname and URL components with no outbound request.

quiz.question: Why preserve the original URL separately from its normalized representation?
options: Normalization can change representation and the source string is evidence
quiz.answer: Normalization can change representation and the source string is evidence
quiz.explanation: The exact source representation may matter for later review and comparison.

summary: URL parsing turns visual suspicion into explicit fields.
Canonicalization must not destroy source evidence.

lessons.title: DNS and Domain Context
lessons.description: Use DNS observations and registration context as supporting evidence rather than verdicts.
learningObjectives: interpret A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, and TXT context
avoid ownership claims from shared hosting

notes.text: A phishing domain can sit on ordinary hosting, shared infrastructure, or compromised services. DNS answers describe observed configuration, while registration information can add historical context. Neither alone proves maliciousness or common control.

items: Record observation time for historical reconstruction.
An IP shared by many domains does not prove common ownership.
A newly registered domain is a clue, not a verdict.

quiz.question: What does two suspicious domains resolving to the same IP establish?
options: Observed infrastructure overlap, but not necessarily common control
That one domain is a subdomain of the other
quiz.answer: Observed infrastructure overlap, but not necessarily common control
quiz.explanation: Shared hosting can create IP overlap without shared ownership.

summary: Infrastructure is strongest when multiple independent signals converge.
Avoid unsupported threat-actor attribution.

lessons.title: Controlled Redirect and Page Analysis
lessons.description: Investigate phishing destinations without risking production credentials or sessions.

notes.text: Controlled workflow

Use an isolated environment without production sessions, browser profiles, or real credentials. Capture the original URL, redirect sequence, final host, page indicators, and collection time. For credential-harvesting pages, never authenticate with real credentials.

items: Treat screenshots as supplemental evidence.
Record the observation timestamp because infrastructure can change.
Separate live behavior observations from static indicator collection.

notes.text: Opening suspicious links from a production endpoint can expose the investigator to the same attack being investigated.

quiz.question: Why should an analyst avoid entering real credentials on a suspected phishing page?
options: It could disclose valid credentials or session material
quiz.answer: It could disclose valid credentials or session material
quiz.explanation: The analysis workflow must not create a new compromise.

summary: Safety is part of evidence collection.
Controlled detonation protects investigators and preserves repeatability.

tasks.title: Normalize Suspicious URLs Safely
tasks.description: Parse controlled URLs and output structured fields.
tasks.problemStatement: Identify hostname, port, userinfo, path, and query fields without discarding the original string.
tasks.hint: Use urllib.parse.urlsplit and keep the raw input.
tasks.solutionCode:
from urllib.parse import urlsplit
import json

raw_url = "https://login.example.invalid@untrusted.invalid/session?next=%2Fhome"
parts = urlsplit(raw_url)
result = {
    "original": raw_url,
    "scheme": parts.scheme,
    "hostname": parts.hostname,
    "port": parts.port,
    "userinfo_present": bool(parts.username),
    "path": parts.path,
    "query": parts.query,
}
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
tasks.solutionExplanation: The utility creates a structured analytical view while preserving the original URL.

modules.title: Attachments, Hashes, and Evidence Objects
modules.description: Preserve and triage attachments as evidence objects with provenance and integrity metadata.

lessons.title: MIME Parts and Attachment Provenance
lessons.description: Understand attachment extraction and source relationships.

notes.text: Attachments should be treated as child artifacts of a source message. Record the parent message identifier, filename, observed MIME type, size, and cryptographic digest before deeper analysis.

items: Extract without executing.
Track nested artifacts as separate objects.
Preserve parent-child relationships so analysts can move back to the source message.

quiz.question: Which metadata best preserves attachment context?
options: Parent message, filename, size, MIME context, and hash
quiz.answer: Parent message, filename, size, MIME context, and hash
quiz.explanation: Those fields preserve provenance, context, and integrity information.

summary: Attachment extraction is evidence handling, not file opening.
Provenance must survive downstream transformations.

lessons.title: Hashing and Exact-Byte Integrity
lessons.description: Use SHA-256 for evidence identification and understand its limits.
learningObjectives: hash source and derived artifacts separately

notes.text: A SHA-256 digest identifies the byte sequence that was hashed. Matching digests support content equality for those bytes, but do not establish authorship, origin, or maliciousness.

from pathlib import Path
import hashlib

data = Path("evidence.eml").read_bytes()
print(hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest())

items: Hash the exact preserved source bytes.
Record algorithm and digest with the evidence record.
Derived copies should have their own digests and provenance.

practicals.title: Hash an Evidence Artifact
practicals.description: Create an evidence record containing the exact byte count and SHA-256 digest of a controlled artifact.
steps: Select a controlled attachment or message file.
Read it as bytes without modifying it.
Calculate a SHA-256 digest using hashlib.
Store the filename, byte count, and digest together.
practicals.solution:
from pathlib import Path
import hashlib

artifact = Path("attachment.bin")
data = artifact.read_bytes()
record = {
    "filename": artifact.name,
    "size_bytes": len(data),
    "sha256": hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest(),
}
print(record)
practicals.output: A compact evidence record showing the artifact name, byte count, and SHA-256 hash.

quiz.question: What does a SHA-256 digest most directly provide?
options: A reproducible identifier for the hashed bytes
quiz.answer: A reproducible identifier for the hashed bytes
quiz.explanation: A digest supports integrity verification and exact-byte correlation.

summary: Hashing supports integrity and correlation, not attribution.
The byte sequence matters.

lessons.title: Archive, Extension, and File-Signature Triage
lessons.description: Analyze disguised files and nested archives without trusting filename extensions.
learningObjectives: compare naming with observed file structure
document password-protected content as a limitation

notes.text: File names can be changed without changing content. Triage should consider the observed file signature, MIME metadata, size, nesting, and archive structure where available. A protected archive remains evidence even when its contents cannot be inspected yet.

items: Do not execute unknown content on the production workstation.
Hash original and derived artifacts separately.
Record failed extraction attempts and reasons.

quiz.question: Why is the extension alone insufficient for file-type triage?
options: Names can be misleading and do not establish underlying structure
quiz.answer: Names can be misleading and do not establish underlying structure
quiz.explanation: An attacker can rename an artifact without changing its underlying content.

summary: File identity is an evidence question, not a naming question.
Nested evidence must remain traceable.

tasks.title: Create an Attachment Evidence Manifest
tasks.description: Generate a manifest for controlled attachment artifacts.
tasks.problemStatement: Record filename, size, hash, and parent relationship for each file.
tasks.hint: Treat every artifact as a separate evidence object.
tasks.solutionCode:
from pathlib import Path
import hashlib

artifact = Path("evidence.eml")
data = artifact.read_bytes()
digest = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
print({"file": artifact.name, "bytes": len(data), "sha256": digest})
tasks.solutionExplanation: The example demonstrates source hashing. The student’s manifest should add explicit parent artifact IDs for nested files.

modules.title: User Interaction and Account Impact
modules.description: Correlate delivery, click, credential, identity, and mailbox evidence without confusing correlation with proof.

lessons.title: Delivery, Open, Click, and Submit States
lessons.description: Differentiate what mail telemetry can and cannot establish.

notes.text: A delivered message proves delivery, not that a person opened or clicked it. Secure-link telemetry, browser records, endpoint events, or provider audit data can provide stronger interaction evidence. Absence of telemetry should be documented as a limitation.

items: State the source and timestamp of each interaction event.
Do not infer click from delivery alone.
Do not infer credential submission from a click alone.

quiz.question: Which observation best supports a phishing-link click?
options: Provider or endpoint telemetry recording a request to the destination
quiz.answer: Provider or endpoint telemetry recording a request to the destination
quiz.explanation: Direct interaction telemetry is stronger evidence of a click than message delivery or content alone.

summary: Phishing investigation requires event-level evidence.
Missing telemetry is an explicit limitation.

lessons.title: Credential Exposure and Identity Correlation
lessons.description: Pivot from the message to identity telemetry when credentials may have been exposed.

notes.text: Identity evidence can include sign-in time, source address, device context, MFA events, password resets, and session changes. A sign-in shortly after a phishing event is a correlation lead; analysts should assess the full identity context before declaring compromise.

items: Normalize timestamps before comparison.
New device or geography can be suspicious but is not proof by itself.
Follow the organization’s approved containment procedure when exposure is credible.

quiz.question: What should follow a credible report that a user entered credentials into a phishing page?
options: Review identity telemetry and follow account-containment procedure
quiz.answer: Review identity telemetry and follow account-containment procedure
quiz.explanation: Potential credential exposure requires identity-focused evidence collection and appropriate containment.

summary: Credential exposure turns a mail investigation into an identity investigation.
Context determines the strength of the correlation.

lessons.title: Mailbox Rules and Post-Compromise Persistence
lessons.description: Investigate mailbox changes that may extend or hide attacker access.
learningObjectives: correlate rule creation with identity events

notes.text: Unexpected external forwarding, hidden-folder rules, or other mailbox changes can be relevant after credential compromise. Review creation time, initiating identity, source device, and business justification before labeling a change malicious.

items: External forwarding is higher risk when it conflicts with policy or user behavior.
Automated workflows can create legitimate rules.
Mailbox evidence should be correlated with identity telemetry.

quiz.question: Which mailbox change deserves priority investigation after suspected compromise?
quiz.answer: Unexpected external forwarding
quiz.explanation: External forwarding may expose future mail and can be used to maintain access or collect information.

summary: Mailbox configuration can reveal impact after the original phishing message.
Persistence hypotheses require timeline and provenance.

tasks.title: Correlate Phishing and Sign-In Events
tasks.description: Identify sign-ins occurring within a configurable window after a phishing event.
tasks.problemStatement: Correlate controlled message and sign-in events by user and UTC time without automatically declaring compromise.
tasks.hint: Make the output a candidate list, not a verdict.
tasks.solutionCode:
from datetime import datetime, timezone

message_time = datetime.fromisoformat("2026-09-07T10:00:00+00:00").astimezone(timezone.utc)
events = [
    {"user": "analyst@example.invalid", "time": "2026-09-07T10:12:00+00:00"},
    {"user": "analyst@example.invalid", "time": "2026-09-07T13:40:00+00:00"},
]
for event in events:
    event_time = datetime.fromisoformat(event["time"]).astimezone(timezone.utc)
    delta = (event_time - message_time).total_seconds()
    if 0 <= delta <= 3600:
        print({**event, "seconds_after_message": int(delta)})
tasks.solutionExplanation: The utility identifies temporal candidates. Analysts must validate source, device, and other context before concluding compromise.

modules.title: Campaign Scoping and Threat Intelligence
modules.description: Expand a message into a campaign and create context-rich indicators suitable for controlled sharing.

lessons.title: Campaign Pivots and Similarity
lessons.description: Use evidence-ranked pivots to identify related phishing messages.

notes.text: Campaign scoping can use exact attachment hashes, URLs, message identifiers, infrastructure, sender patterns, lure themes, and time windows. Each pivot has a different false-positive profile, so inclusion decisions should record why the event is considered related.

items: Exact file hash is strong for identical bytes.
Generic subjects and branding are weaker pivots.
Shared IP infrastructure needs additional context.

quiz.question: Which pivot is strongest for identifying identical attachment content?
quiz.answer: SHA-256
quiz.explanation: An exact hash match strongly supports identical bytes, subject to collection context.

summary: Campaign scope should be explainable event by event.
Pivots should be selected for evidentiary value, not convenience.

lessons.title: Indicator Quality, Confidence, and Attribution
lessons.description: Create operationally useful indicators without overstating actor attribution.

notes.text: An indicator can be a domain, URL, IP address, email address, hash, or message identifier. Operational quality improves when indicators are precise, time-scoped, and linked to evidence. Confidence should reflect independent corroboration rather than repetition of one source.

items: A technical indicator does not automatically identify an adversary.
Negative evidence can reduce confidence.
Actor attribution requires a higher evidence threshold than infrastructure identification.

quiz.question: What most strengthens confidence in an indicator assessment?
quiz.answer: Independent corroboration
quiz.explanation: Independent evidence sources reduce reliance on one incomplete observation.

summary: Confidence is a reasoned judgment that should be auditable.
Indicator context is as important as the value itself.

lessons.title: STIX, TAXII, and TLP 2.0
lessons.description: Understand structured intelligence exchange and information-sharing boundaries.
learningObjectives: recognize when structured phishing intelligence is useful

notes.text: STIX 2.1 is a language for expressing cyber threat and observable information. TAXII 2.1 specifies an application-layer protocol and resources for communicating cyber threat information. FIRST TLP 2.0 labels sharing boundaries with TLP:RED, TLP:AMBER, TLP:GREEN, and TLP:CLEAR.

items: Do not represent a custom JSON record as a standards-compliant STIX bundle.
TLP communicates handling expectations, not maliciousness.
Preserve source and confidence fields in intelligence records.

quiz.question: What is TAXII 2.1 primarily designed to do?
options: Communicate cyber threat information through a defined protocol
quiz.answer: Communicate cyber threat information through a defined protocol
quiz.explanation: TAXII defines a protocol and API resources for exchanging cyber threat information.

summary: Structured intelligence improves interoperability when semantics are explicit.
TLP is a handling label, not a verdict.

tasks.title: Create a Controlled Threat-Intelligence Record
tasks.description: Produce a small JSON intelligence record for a phishing campaign.
tasks.problemStatement: Include indicators, confidence, evidence references, and a TLP label while explicitly using an internal schema rather than claiming full STIX compliance.
tasks.hint: Keep indicator value, source evidence, and confidence as separate fields.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The record demonstrates provenance and sharing metadata without pretending to implement the STIX standard.

modules.title: Containment, Remediation, and Validation
modules.description: Translate findings into proportionate operational actions and verify that remediation worked.

lessons.title: Evidence-to-Action Decisions
lessons.description: Select containment actions based on evidence, impact, and authorization.

notes.text: Containment can involve mail search and removal, indicator blocks, session revocation, credential resets, or increased monitoring. The appropriate action depends on evidence quality, likely impact, organizational authority, and the risk of disruption.

items: High-confidence credential exposure can justify rapid identity containment.
Unconfirmed indicators may warrant monitoring or scoped blocking.
Every action should have a validation method.

quiz.question: What makes a containment action auditable?
options: Rationale, owner, evidence basis, and validation method
quiz.answer: Rationale, owner, evidence basis, and validation method
quiz.explanation: Those fields allow later reviewers to understand why the action occurred and whether it worked.

summary: Containment is a decision process tied to evidence.
Operational actions must be traceable and authorized.

lessons.title: Mail Search and False-Positive Control
lessons.description: Design remediation searches that minimize accidental removal of legitimate mail.

notes.text: Exact indicators such as a message identifier, attachment hash, URL, or combination of features can support targeted remediation. Broad subject or brand searches can overmatch, so previewing scope and recording result counts are important controls.

items: Keep the query or predicate in the case record.
Use multiple conditions when one indicator is noisy.
Validate the post-action population.

quiz.question: Why preview a remediation search before destructive action?
quiz.answer: To reduce false-positive deletion risk
quiz.explanation: Previewing lets the analyst validate the intended scope before removal.

summary: Message-remediation searches are operational evidence.
False-positive control protects the business as well as the investigation.

lessons.title: Post-Containment Validation and Closure
lessons.description: Verify that remediation reduced exposure and document residual uncertainty.

notes.text: Closure is stronger when it includes repeat searches, block validation, identity review, and monitoring for reappearance. A clean result is time-dependent, so the report should include validation time and residual limitations.

items: Do not equate “not found” with “never existed.”
Re-check campaign variants and alternate indicators.
Keep response timestamps and validation evidence.

quiz.question: Which is a useful post-remediation check?
options: Repeat the scoped search and verify the expected result
quiz.answer: Repeat the scoped search and verify the expected result
quiz.explanation: A repeat query provides direct evidence about the success of the intended remediation scope.

summary: Validation converts response actions into evidence of outcome.
Closure should preserve residual risk rather than hide it.

tasks.title: Write a Phishing Containment Runbook
tasks.description: Create a JSON decision runbook for suspicious, confirmed, and credential-exposure scenarios.
tasks.problemStatement: Define actions, ownership assumptions, and validation checks for each evidence state.
tasks.hint: For every action state what evidence justifies it and how success will be verified.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The runbook separates evidence state from action and makes validation explicit.

modules.title: Detection Engineering and SOC Metrics
modules.description: Use investigation lessons to improve phishing detections, test them safely, and measure investigation quality.

lessons.title: From Investigation to Detection Logic
lessons.description: Translate investigation findings into robust detection features.

notes.text: Detection features can include authentication anomalies, suspicious URL structures, lookalike domains, unusual mailbox changes, and campaign context. A good detection describes observable conditions and should not depend on one exact subject or sender string.

items: Use multiple relevant signals when one feature is noisy.
Document why the feature maps to observed behavior.
Keep destructive response automation separately governed.

quiz.question: Which approach is generally more resilient to simple campaign changes?
quiz.answer: Multiple relevant evidence signals
quiz.explanation: Multi-signal logic is generally less brittle than one literal campaign artifact.

summary: Detection should encode durable evidence patterns.
A detection is not automatically a response action.

lessons.title: Detection Test Design
lessons.description: Create positive, negative, and edge cases for phishing detection tuning.

notes.text: Detection tuning is safer when test cases include intended phishing positives, benign negatives, and ambiguous edge conditions. An external Reply-To can be a useful example of an anomaly that needs review rather than automatic blocking.

items: Freeze expected outcomes before the test.
Keep benign examples representative of real mail flow.
Record why tuning changed after a test.

quiz.question: Why include benign negative test cases?
options: To measure false positives and protect legitimate mail flow
quiz.answer: To measure false positives and protect legitimate mail flow
quiz.explanation: Negative cases reveal overmatching and support safer tuning.

summary: Good tuning uses evidence from both false positives and false negatives.
Ambiguity can legitimately route to analyst review.

lessons.title: Phishing Investigation Metrics
lessons.description: Define measurable metrics for speed, evidence quality, and outcome.
learningObjectives: include a denominator and time window

notes.text: Useful measures can include median triage time, time to campaign scope, percentage of cases preserving original artifacts, recurrence after remediation, and false-positive rate. Each metric needs a population, time period, and calculation method.

items: Raw volume is not a complete performance measure.
Evidence-quality metrics should reflect preservation and reproducibility.
Document exclusions and data gaps.

quiz.question: Which metric directly evaluates evidence preservation?
options: Percentage of cases with preserved and hashed original artifacts
quiz.answer: Percentage of cases with preserved and hashed original artifacts
quiz.explanation: That metric evaluates whether investigations retained reproducible source evidence.

summary: Metrics should support decisions, not just dashboards.
A denominator and time window make a metric interpretable.

tasks.title: Build a Phishing Detection Test Matrix
tasks.description: Represent positive, negative, and edge test cases as JSON.
tasks.problemStatement: Define expected alert states and rationale for controlled phishing detection tests.
tasks.hint: Include at least one benign case that resembles the malicious pattern.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The matrix makes expected outcomes explicit and supports repeatable tuning.

modules.title: Reporting and Communication
modules.description: Produce technically precise and audience-appropriate phishing reports with evidence, confidence, timeline, impact, and limitations.

lessons.title: Evidence-to-Finding Writing
lessons.description: Convert observations into concise, traceable findings.

notes.text: A defensible finding states the observed fact, the analytical interpretation, and the operational implication. For example, an Authentication-Results dkim=fail value is an observation; concern about claimed domain authentication is an interpretation. Avoid collapsing them into a single unsupported statement.

items: Use exact field names where wording matters.
Reference source artifacts and timestamps.
Do not turn an absence of evidence into evidence of absence.

quiz.question: Which is a direct observation?
quiz.answer: Authentication-Results contains dkim=fail.
quiz.explanation: That statement reports a directly observed field value.

summary: Precision is more valuable than dramatic language.
Readers should be able to trace each conclusion back to evidence.

lessons.title: Timeline Construction
lessons.description: Build a normalized timeline from message and telemetry events.

notes.text: A phishing timeline can combine message Date, Received fields, provider audit logs, endpoint data, identity events, and response actions. Preserve the original timestamp and source while generating a normalized comparison view.

items: Message Date is not delivery time by definition.
Received events represent processing points.
Different systems can have different clock behavior or delays.

quiz.question: Why retain the original timezone when normalizing to UTC?
options: It makes the normalized conversion auditable
quiz.answer: It makes the normalized conversion auditable
quiz.explanation: The source context lets a reviewer reconstruct the normalization.

summary: A timeline is a synthesis of multiple clocks and sources.
Every event needs provenance and context.

lessons.title: Executive and Technical Reporting
lessons.description: Adapt the same case to technical and leadership audiences without changing the facts.

notes.text: Executives generally need impact, affected scope, decisions, and residual risk. Technical responders need evidence, indicators, timelines, searches, and limitations. Both views should derive from the same case record and maintain the same factual conclusion.

items: Simplify jargon, not evidence.
Keep material uncertainty visible.
Use the technical appendix for reproducibility.

quiz.question: What must remain consistent across executive and technical reports?
options: Underlying evidence-based conclusion and material uncertainty
quiz.answer: Underlying evidence-based conclusion and material uncertainty
quiz.explanation: Different audiences can receive different detail, but not different facts.

summary: Audience changes presentation, not truth.
Executive summaries should remain consistent with technical evidence.

tasks.title: Generate a Defensible Phishing Report
tasks.description: Produce a machine-readable report with findings and limitations.
tasks.problemStatement: Represent assessment, confidence, evidence-backed findings, impact, actions, and limitations.
tasks.hint: Each finding should carry evidence, confidence, impact, and action.
tasks.solutionCode:
import json

report = {
    "case": "PHISH-2026-001",
    "assessment": "Malicious phishing",
    "confidence": "High",
    "findings": [
        {
            "name": "Authentication anomaly",
            "evidence": "Controlled Authentication-Results data records dkim=fail.",
            "confidence": "High",
            "impact": "Visible sender identity requires additional validation.",
            "action": "Scope related messages and review sender infrastructure."
        }
    ],
    "limitations": ["Mailbox-side delivery logs were unavailable in the controlled dataset."]
}
print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))
tasks.solutionExplanation: The example uses a compact schema that preserves the evidence-to-action relationship.

modules.title: Final Capstone — End-to-End Phishing Investigation
modules.description: Complete one realistic controlled phishing case from evidence preservation through final response reporting. This module contains the final project and no separate module tasks.

lessons.title: Capstone Planning and Evidence Gates
lessons.description: Plan the capstone before analysis and define the evidence and completion gates.

notes.text: Capstone gates

The controlled dataset should contain an EML message, URL artifacts, controlled attachment samples or metadata, and synthetic mail/identity events. Establish an evidence manifest before interpretation. Success means the final report can explain what is known, what is inferred, what was done, and what remains unknown.

items: Preserve → analyze → scope → assess impact → respond → validate → report.
No real credentials, personal data, or live phishing infrastructure are required.

quiz.question: What is the first capstone gate?
quiz.answer: Evidence preservation and scope
quiz.explanation: The case begins by establishing scope and protecting source evidence.

summary: The capstone evaluates investigation reasoning across the full workflow.

project.name: End-to-End Phishing Investigation Case
project.description: Investigate a controlled phishing campaign from preserved email through final SOC reporting using synthetic telemetry and non-live infrastructure.
steps: 1. Freeze the controlled dataset and hash every source artifact.
2. Parse the EML and preserve identity, authentication, and routing fields.
3. Analyze SPF/DKIM/DMARC results without treating them as a universal verdict.
4. Extract and normalize URLs without using production credentials or sessions.
5. Build attachment evidence objects with hashes and parent relationships.
6. Correlate synthetic click/sign-in/mailbox events with the phishing timeline.
7. Expand campaign scope using evidence-ranked pivots and confidence labels.
8. Map the observed delivery method to the correct MITRE ATT&CK phishing sub-technique.
9. Build a proportionate containment plan and validation checklist.
10. Produce a final technical report and executive summary with explicit limitations.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from email import policy
from email.parser import BytesParser
from hashlib import sha256
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import urlsplit
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import json
import re

@dataclass
class Finding:
    name: str
    observation: str
    assessment: str
    confidence: str
    evidence: list[str]

def parse_message(path: Path) -> tuple[dict, str]:
    raw = path.read_bytes()
    digest = sha256(raw).hexdigest()
    message = BytesParser(policy=policy.default).parsebytes(raw)
    record = {
        "filename": path.name,
        "sha256": digest,
        "from": message.get("From"),
        "to": message.get("To"),
        "reply_to": message.get("Reply-To"),
        "message_id": message.get("Message-ID"),
        "authentication_results": message.get("Authentication-Results"),
        "received": message.get_all("Received", []),
    }
    return record, message.as_string()

def extract_urls(message_text: str) -> list[dict]:
    results = []
    candidates = re.findall(r'https?://[^\s<>"\']+', message_text)
    for value in candidates:
        parsed = urlsplit(value)
        results.append({
            "original": value,
            "scheme": parsed.scheme,
            "hostname": parsed.hostname,
            "username_present": bool(parsed.username),
            "port": parsed.port,
            "path": parsed.path,
            "query": parsed.query,
        })
    return results

def build_investigation(eml_path: Path, artifact_paths: list[Path]) -> dict:
    message_record, message_text = parse_message(eml_path)
    artifacts = []
    for path in artifact_paths:
        raw = path.read_bytes()
        artifacts.append({
            "filename": path.name,
            "size_bytes": len(raw),
            "sha256": sha256(raw).hexdigest(),
        })

    findings = []
    auth = message_record.get("authentication_results")
    if auth:
        findings.append(asdict(Finding(
            name="Authentication result review",
            observation=str(auth),
            assessment="Authentication results are evidence for contextual analysis; they are not a stand-alone verdict of maliciousness.",
            confidence="Medium",
            evidence=["Authentication-Results header"]
        )))

    return {
        "case": message_record,
        "urls": extract_urls(message_text),
        "artifacts": artifacts,
        "findings": findings,
        "generated_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    case = build_investigation(Path("evidence.eml"), [Path("evidence.eml")])
    Path("investigation.json").write_text(json.dumps(case, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    print("Created investigation.json from preserved evidence and offline analysis.")

project.explanation: The capstone uses controlled artifacts so students practice realistic investigation without live attacker infrastructure. The workflow starts with evidence preservation, then moves through standards-based message analysis, safe URL and attachment triage, identity correlation, campaign scoping, operational response planning, validation, and final reporting. Each conclusion must be traceable to an artifact or telemetry record, while limitations remain explicit.
